Best time to trade US100? 2,069 entry/exit windows tested

One of the most common day-trading questions is “when should I enter and when should I exit?” US100 trades almost 24 hours a day, pausing only from 17:00 to 18:00 New York time, so this post sweeps the entire session: from the 18:00 evening open to the next afternoon, entering at a fixed New York time and exiting at a fixed time, spanning midnight where needed, with no signals at all, 2,069 sets across long and short. The questions: which windows have an edge on their own? Are the good results a plateau or a single island? How do long and short differ? Everything is computed in volatility mode: each trade’s P&L divided by the daily ATR(72) at exit (the Average True Range over 72 New York daily bars, about 60 trading days), summed, as if every trade carried the same volatility risk; see the research glossary.

Conclusion

Longs make money in most windows, and the two best regions are entering after the 18:00 evening open and holding overnight, and entering around 11:00 New York time. Shorts make money in only a few windows, concentrated on an 11:00 exit. Of 1,034 long sets, 938931 have a profit factor above 1; of 1,035 short sets, only 96103 do. By score (expectancy per unit of adverse movement), the best long is enter 18:00, exit 04:00 the next day, and the best short is enter 04:30, exit 05:00, but the short edge is thin.

  1. Longs entering at the 18:00 open form a plateau: entering at 18:00 and exiting at 04:00 the next day (the whole Asian session) has a profit factor of 1.2291.216, and holding until 14:00 the next day totals +44.4 vol+74.1%, the highest total return of any long set. Evidence: Parameter stability
  2. With the same 18:00 long entry, exiting at 04:00 has a max drawdown of −4.9 vol−10.2%, while holding to 14:00 has a max drawdown of −17.8 vol−36.3%: the extra return comes with a much deeper drawdown. Evidence: Risk
  3. The top-scoring short, 04:30–05:00, has a profit factor of only 1.1321.129; the shorts with higher total returns all exit at 11:00, such as 10:00–11:00 with a profit factor of 1.1261.102. Evidence: Returns

That is the conclusion. Each section below is the evidence for one claim; follow the sections or the evidence links into the strategy report for the data on every parameter set.

How do we compare 2,069 time windows?

US100 pauses only from 17:00 to 18:00 New York time each day (00:00–01:00 FTMO server time). A session runs from the 18:00 open to 17:00 the next day, and the session that opens Sunday evening at 18:00 belongs to Monday. Each set is a fixed clock: in every session it enters at a given New York time and exits at a given time within the same session, so it can span midnight (for example, enter 22:00 and exit 06:00), but never holds through the daily break or the weekend. Entries run from 18:00 to 16:00 and exits up to 16:30, in 30-minute steps, with long and short tested separately.

The score used to pick windows is the average return per trade divided by the average Maximum Adverse Excursion (MAE), meaning “how much expectancy you get for each unit of adverse movement you sit through.” It is then averaged with the neighboring sets that enter or exit 30 minutes earlier or later, so the result must hold up even when you enter or exit one bar late. The average return must also be positive in both 2022–2024 and 2025–2026.

Which windows are best for longs?

938931 long sets have a profit factor above 1. Part of this is simply the index’s long-term rise: the longer you hold, the more of the uptrend you capture. The more informative question is where results are especially good. In the chart below, rows are entry times and columns are exit times (both counted from the 18:00 open), and each cell is the profit factor:

Long: profit factor by entry × exit

Profit factor across parameter combinations; outlined cells are the sets the article mentions. Green is above the median of all sets, red below. Good neighbors mean a plateau; a single good cell means an island. Pick one to three parameters.

Other parameters: fixed at one of the sets the article mentions, or the median of all parameter sets (lighter cells have few sets)

Two regions stand out: the top few rows (entering after the open, 18:00–19:30) and entries around 11:00. Both are plateaus, not single cells. Entering at 18:00 and exiting at 04:00 the next day holds only through the Asian session, with a profit factor of 1.2291.216 and 44 / 55 positive years. During the day, entering at 11:00 and exiting at 16:00 totals +30.6 vol+60.5%, with 55 / 55 positive years.

Are there any good windows for shorts?

Only 96103 short sets have a profit factor above 1; in most windows, shorting loses money:

Short: profit factor by entry × exit

Profit factor across parameter combinations; outlined cells are the sets the article mentions. Green is above the median of all sets, red below. Good neighbors mean a plateau; a single good cell means an island. Pick one to three parameters.

Other parameters: fixed at one of the sets the article mentions, or the median of all parameter sets (lighter cells have few sets)

The profitable shorts cluster in the 11:00 exit column, while the good daytime long windows start at 11:00. Both point to a turn around 11:00: prices lean lower before 11:00 and higher after. Entering short at 10:00 and exiting at 11:00 has a profit factor of 1.1261.102 and 44 / 55 positive years. The top-scoring 04:30–05:00 short totals only +4.1 vol+6.8%, which the spread may well wipe out.

With the same 11:00 long entry, a later exit generally means a higher total return and a deeper max drawdown. The evening entry behaves the same way: entering at 18:00 and exiting at 04:00 has a max drawdown of −4.9 vol−10.2%, while holding until 14:00 the next day has a max drawdown of −17.8 vol−36.3%. The score prefers the former: it earns more expectancy per unit of adverse movement.

Read with care
  • Returns are the simple sum of per-trade results in volatility-normalized mode (each trade’s P&L divided by the daily ATR at exit), ignoring position size and compounding.
  • All 2,069 sets were compared and selected on the same sample (January 28, 2022 to September 2026), so every result is in-sample.
  • Neighboring windows mostly overlap in holding time, so these are not 2,069 independent trials; highly correlated sets should be treated as variants of one hypothesis.
  • Part of why longs generally make money is that the index rose over the sample period; this post does not subtract the market’s gain.
  • Spread, commissions and slippage are not included; spreads are usually wider in the evening and the Asian session, and the edge in short windows is the easiest to lose to costs.
  • On early-close holidays there is no bar at the scheduled exit time, so the trade exits at the next session’s open (18:00); on a Friday early close it holds over the weekend. These trades are about 1% of the total.
  • The Long 22:00 entry, 06:00 exit set could not be written to the backtest results and is left blank on the heatmap.
  • This is not investment advice.

What does this mean?

Looking at time alone, the US100 edge is mainly on the long side, in two regions: entering after the 18:00 evening open and holding overnight until the Asian session ends, and entering around 11:00 New York time and holding into the afternoon. Both are plateaus, not islands. Short opportunities are rare; the most consistent is the decline from the morning into 11:00. This is only the effect of trading the window every day; the same window performs very differently by weekday and Market Profile state, see “US100 clock windows by weekday × Market Profile”. Delayed entries, stops and position sizing are added layer by layer on the selected windows in “The US100 clock strategy tree”.

Questions this study answers

Which US100 entry and exit windows have an edge on their own?

Most long windows make money, and the best two regions are entering after the 18:00 evening open and holding overnight, and entering around 11:00 New York time into the afternoon; 938931 of 1,034 long sets have a profit factor above 1. Entering at 18:00 and exiting at 04:00 has a profit factor of 1.2291.216, and 11:00 to 16:00 totals +30.6 vol+60.5%.

Are the good results a plateau or a single island?

Both long regions are plateaus: the rows entering just after the open (18:00–19:30) and the area around an 11:00 entry are high as a whole, not single cells. The profitable shorts also cluster in the 11:00 exit column rather than in scattered cells.

How do long and short differ?

Only 96103 of 1,035 short sets have a profit factor above 1, and only 11 are positive every year, against 11272 longs. The most consistent shorts enter in the morning and exit at 11:00, such as 10:00–11:00 with a profit factor of 1.1261.102.

Questions raised along the way

How is selection bias reduced across two thousand windows?

The score (mean return ÷ mean MAE) is averaged with the neighboring windows 30 minutes earlier and later on both entry and exit, so entering or exiting one bar late must also work, and both 2022–2024 and 2025–2026 must have a positive mean return. Neighboring windows mostly overlap in holding time, so the results remain in-sample and need new data to confirm them.

Is the broad long edge just the index rising?

Partly. The longer a window holds, the more of the rise it captures, and this post does not subtract the market’s gain, so the informative part is which windows stand out. Later studies add a same-window hold of US100 as a control that each window must beat.

What does the higher return of longer windows cost in risk?

Entering long at 18:00, exiting at 04:00 has a max drawdown of −4.9 vol−10.2%, and holding to 14:00 the next day −17.8 vol−36.3%. The score prefers the former: more expected return per unit of adverse move.

Method and data

Research setup, data and calculations; the identifiers needed to reproduce the study are under data sources.

Research setup
Article type
Parameter sweep
Instrument
US100.cash
Direction
Both directions
Bars
US100 (FTMO) 15-minute bars, New York time
Session
Daily break is 17:00–18:00 New York time (00:00–01:00 FTMO server time); a session runs from the 18:00 open to 17:00 the next day, and the Sunday 18:00 open belongs to Monday
Entry and exit
Fixed clock: in every session (Monday to Friday), enter at the given New York time and exit at the given time within the same session; trades can span midnight but never the daily break or the weekend; no stop loss, take profit or other signals
Sweep
Long and short × entry 18:00–16:00 × exit (from 30 minutes after entry) up to 16:30, in 30-minute steps, 2,070 sets in total; Long 22:00 entry, 06:00 exit is missing because its backtest results could not be written, leaving 2,069 sets
Score
Average return per trade ÷ average Maximum Adverse Excursion (MAE), then averaged with the neighboring sets 30 minutes earlier and later on both entry and exit; the average return must be positive in both 2022–2024 and 2025–2026
Analyzer mode
Volatility-normalized by default: each trade's P&L is divided by the daily ATR (72 bars, previous completed day) at exit and summed; switch to percentage at the top of the page
Sample
Sessions from January 28, 2022 (once daily ATR72 is available) through September 23, 2026
Costs
Not included
Parameters
Direction: Long / Short; Entry (New York): 45 values, full list in the strategy report; Exit (New York): 45 values, full list in the strategy report
Return calculation
Volatility-normalized: Sum of per-trade P&L ÷ volatility at exit (exit_volatility); Percentage: Sum of per-trade returns (simple)
